issue: fs.readFileSync inside async Express handler — blocks Node.js event loop on every GET /api/feature-flags request
evidence: const raw = fs.readFileSync(FLAGS_PATH, 'utf-8')
estimated_impact: Blocks event loop for ~1-5ms per call (disk I/O). Under 100 req/s, this adds 100-500ms of cumulative blocking per second, starving other requests. All concurrent requests queue behind the synchronous read.
recommendation: Read features.json once at module load time and cache in memory. Use fs.watch or a simple TTL cache for invalidation. Alternatively use fs.promises.readFile with await.

issue: fs.readFileSync + fs.writeFileSync in POST /api/feature-flags/:name/state — double synchronous file I/O (read then write) blocks event loop on every state change
evidence: const raw = fs.readFileSync(FLAGS_PATH, 'utf-8'); ... fs.writeFileSync(FLAGS_PATH, JSON.stringify(flags, null, 2), 'utf-8')
estimated_impact: ~2-10ms of event-loop blocking per state-change request. Also reads descriptions.json synchronously on line 93. Three sync I/O operations in a single request handler.
recommendation: Use async fs.promises.readFile/writeFile, or better: keep flags in an in-memory cache and write through asynchronously.

issue: fs.readFileSync + fs.writeFileSync in POST /api/feature-flags/:name/traffic — same double sync I/O pattern as setFeatureState
evidence: const raw = fs.readFileSync(FLAGS_PATH, 'utf-8'); ... fs.writeFileSync(FLAGS_PATH, JSON.stringify(flags, null, 2), 'utf-8')
estimated_impact: ~2-10ms event-loop block per traffic-adjustment request. Combined with the descriptions.json read on line 132, three sync I/O ops per request.
recommendation: Same as setFeatureState — use in-memory cache with async write-through.

issue: getFeatureFlagByName reads BOTH features.json AND descriptions.json synchronously for a single flag lookup — wasteful double file read
evidence: const raw = fs.readFileSync(FLAGS_PATH, 'utf-8'); ... const descRaw = fs.readFileSync(DESCS_PATH, 'utf-8')
estimated_impact: Two sync file reads (~2-8ms) to return a single flag. Every frontend poll cycle hits this endpoint.
recommendation: Cache both files in memory at module scope. Invalidate on change.

issue: getOrders (GET /api/orders, admin) returns ALL orders with .populate('user', 'id name') — no pagination, no limit
evidence: const orders = await Order.find({}).populate('user', 'id name')
estimated_impact: With 10K orders, each with 5 embedded orderItems, this serializes ~50K+ items into JSON per request. Response payload can exceed 5-10MB. p95 latency grows linearly: +500ms at 1K orders, +5s at 10K orders. Memory spike on both server and client.
recommendation: Add pagination (page/pageSize) matching the getProducts pattern. Add .limit() and .select() to reduce fields.

issue: getMyOrders (GET /api/orders/myorders) returns ALL orders for a user with no pagination
evidence: const orders = await Order.find({ user: req.user._id })
estimated_impact: For a frequent buyer with 500+ orders, each containing embedded orderItems, the response payload grows unbounded. No .select() to limit fields — returns full documents with all orderItems arrays.
recommendation: Add pagination and .select() to exclude heavy fields like orderItems if not needed in list view.

issue: getUsers (GET /api/users, admin) returns ALL users with no pagination and no field exclusion — passwords are excluded by the model but all other fields are returned
evidence: const users = await User.find({})
estimated_impact: With 10K users, returns full user documents. Each document includes name, email, isAdmin, timestamps. Response grows linearly — ~500KB at 10K users. Slower than orders but still unbounded.
recommendation: Add pagination and .select('name email isAdmin') to limit returned fields in list view.

issue: No explicit index on User.email — login (findOne({email})) and registration (findOne({email})) perform collection scans on large datasets
evidence: email: { type: String, required: true, unique: true }
estimated_impact: Mongoose unique: true creates a unique index, so this is partially mitigated. However, the Product.name regex search (productController.js:12-18) and Order.user query (orderController.js:105) have no indexes. Product.name $regex with $options 'i' cannot use an index efficiently — full collection scan on every search.
recommendation: Add text index on Product.name and category: schema.index({ name: 'text', category: 'text' }). Add index on Order.user for the myorders query: schema.index({ user: 1 }).

issue: No index on Order.user field — getMyOrders query (find({ user: req.user._id })) does a collection scan
evidence: user: { type: mongoose.Schema.Types.ObjectId, required: true, ref: 'User' }
estimated_impact: With 100K orders, a collection scan on every /myorders request adds +200-500ms. This is a hot path for every logged-in user.
recommendation: Add schema.index({ user: 1 }) to orderModel.js.

issue: protect middleware does a DB query (User.findById) on EVERY authenticated request — no caching of the user lookup
evidence: req.user = await User.findById(decoded.id).select('-password')
estimated_impact: Every API call that uses protect middleware (orders, profile, admin actions) incurs an extra DB roundtrip. At 100 req/s, this is 100 unnecessary DB queries per second. ~5-15ms added per request. The JWT already contains the user ID and isAdmin — the DB query is only needed to check if the user still exists / hasn't been deleted.
recommendation: Short-term: cache user lookups in an in-memory LRU cache (e.g., 60s TTL). Long-term: move admin check to a short-lived token claim + periodic refresh, or use Redis for session data.

issue: Full Bootstrap CSS (176KB) imported synchronously in index.js — entire framework loaded even though only ~30% of classes are used
evidence: import './bootstrap.min.css' (176,708 bytes / 176KB)
estimated_impact: +176KB to the CSS bundle. On 3G (1.6 Mbps), this adds ~880ms to first paint. Bootstrap CSS is render-blocking. Only a subset of components are used (Table, Card, Button, Form, Navbar, Carousel, etc.).
recommendation: Use a tree-shaken Bootstrap build (e.g., bootstrap/scss imports of only needed components) or replace with a lighter utility CSS framework. At minimum, defer-load non-critical Bootstrap styles.

issue: No code splitting or lazy loading — all 16 screens and all components are bundled into a single JS chunk and loaded upfront
evidence: import HomeScreen from './screens/HomeScreen'; import ProductScreen from './screens/ProductScreen'; ... (16 screen imports + 12 component imports, all static)
estimated_impact: All screens (including heavy ones like FeatureFlagListScreen at 484 lines, OrderListScreen, etc.) are in the initial bundle. Estimated +200-400KB of JS that could be split. On 3G, this adds ~1-2s to initial load time.
recommendation: Use React.lazy() + Suspense to code-split routes. Each screen becomes a separate chunk loaded on demand. This is the standard pattern for React Router 5.

issue: Route /top registered AFTER /:id — getTopProducts is unreachable because ':id' captures 'top' as a parameter
evidence: router.route('/:id/reviews').post(protect, createProductReview); router.get('/top', getTopProducts);
estimated_impact: GET /api/products/top triggers getProductById('top') instead of getTopProducts. This causes a failed MongoDB ObjectId cast on every carousel load. The error is caught by asyncHandler, returning 500 or 'Product not found'. ProductCarousel component likely shows error state or empty. Impact: homepage carousel always broken + wasted DB query.
recommendation: Move router.get('/top', getTopProducts) BEFORE router.route('/:id') in productRoutes.js. Express matches routes in registration order.

issue: createProductReview loads the full product document (including all reviews) to check for duplicates and recalculate rating — O(n) scan of reviews array on every review submission
evidence: const alreadyReviewed = product.reviews.find(r => r.user.toString() === req.user._id.toString()); ... product.rating = product.reviews.reduce((acc, item) => item.rating + acc, 0) / product.reviews.length
estimated_impact: For a popular product with 500 reviews, this loads 500 embedded sub-documents into memory and scans them linearly. The .reduce() is a second full pass. With 10 reviews this is negligible, but grows linearly. ~+2ms per 100 reviews.
recommendation: Use a single-pass loop for both check and sum. Or better: use a $elemMatch query to check existence server-side and an aggregation $avg for rating. This avoids loading the full reviews array.

issue: Aggressive polling (every 2 seconds for 10 seconds) after every feature flag action — 5 sequential HTTP requests to GET /api/feature-flags, each triggering sync file reads on backend
evidence: pollingRef.current = setInterval(() => { dispatch(listFeatureFlags()) }, 2000); setTimeout(() => { if (pollingRef.current) clearInterval(pollingRef.current) }, 10000)
estimated_impact: Each poll triggers 2x fs.readFileSync on the backend (features.json + descriptions.json). 5 polls = 10 sync file reads in 10 seconds. If multiple admins interact simultaneously, the polling compounds. Combined with the blocking I/O finding, this creates a burst of event-loop blocks.
recommendation: Reduce poll interval to 5-10s. Better: use WebSocket or SSE for real-time flag updates instead of polling. Or cache flags in memory on the backend so polling is cheap.

issue: Deep clone of entire flags object on every Redux update via JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(flags)) — unnecessary full-structure copy
evidence: setLocalFlags(JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(flags)))
estimated_impact: With 25 feature flags and descriptions, the JSON round-trip is ~10-20KB per update. This runs on every flags fetch (including polls). Minor for 25 flags but the pattern is wasteful — Redux already returns a new state object. The parse/stringify adds ~1-2ms of main-thread blocking per poll cycle.
recommendation: Use structuredClone() (faster) or simply spread the object: setLocalFlags({...flags}). Since the Redux state already creates new references on updates, the deep clone may be unnecessary — verify if mutations are actually occurring.

issue: Product listing executes two separate DB queries (countDocuments + find) — not pipelined, runs sequentially
evidence: const count = await Product.countDocuments({ ...keyword }); const products = await Product.find({ ...keyword }).limit(pageSize).skip(...)
estimated_impact: Two sequential DB round-trips for every product listing page. With a regex search query, both scans the same data. Combined p95 impact: ~20-40ms (2x 10-20ms queries). Could be reduced to a single query with a $facet aggregation.
recommendation: Use Promise.all([countQuery, dataQuery]) to run both in parallel, or use a single $facet aggregation to get count and data in one round-trip.

issue: getTopProducts (GET /api/products/top) runs a full sort by rating on every homepage load — no caching on a deterministic, rarely-changing query
evidence: const products = await Product.find({}).sort({ rating: -1 }).limit(3)
estimated_impact: Every homepage visit triggers a MongoDB sort operation. With 1000 products, this is a sorted scan. The top-3 products rarely change. ~5-15ms per homepage load. If the route ordering bug is fixed, this could be called frequently.
recommendation: Cache the top products result in memory with a 5-10 minute TTL. Invalidate on product create/update/delete.

issue: Quantity selector creates an Array of size countInStock and spreads all keys — if countInStock is large (e.g., 9999), creates 9999 <option> DOM elements
evidence: {[...Array(product.countInStock).keys()].map((x) => (<option key={x + 1} value={x + 1}>{x + 1}</option>))}
estimated_impact: If countInStock is set to a large value (admin error or data import), renders thousands of <option> elements, causing significant DOM bloat and laggy dropdown. Normal case (count < 100) is fine.
recommendation: Cap the rendered options at a reasonable max (e.g., 99 or 100) and add a text input fallback for larger quantities.

issue: Redux DevTools enabled in production via composeWithDevTools — adds overhead to every dispatched action in all environments
evidence: const store = createStore(reducer, initialState, composeWithDevTools(applyMiddleware(...middleware)))
estimated_impact: composeWithDevTools wraps every dispatch with devtools instrumentation. In production, this persists action history in memory, growing unbounded. For a session with 200+ actions (browsing products, cart operations), this retains all action objects and states in memory. ~+5-10MB memory overhead per session.
recommendation: Conditionally apply DevTools only in development: composeWithDevTools(applyMiddleware(...middleware)) only if NODE_ENV === 'development', else applyMiddleware(...middleware).
